data.title: Waymo’s Next Target: Singapore
data.description:
Waymo has expanded its robotaxi service across the United States quite significantly in 2026. It’s not yet covering a huge portion of the population, but it’s operating in more than a dozen major cities already. As it expanded further and further in the US, though, I started wondering how hard it would be for the company to grow into other countries and how much it would try to do so.

Now, however, we’ve got news of it moving into the UK, into Germany, into Japan next year, and the latest news is its next foreign target: Singapore.

The Singapore launched isn’t around the corner. It’s planned for 2028, not next year. However, that also shows us the deliberate, careful approach Waymo takes and its long-term planning. And does anyone doubt Waymo will actually launch service in the unique island city-state in 2028?

Why announce this so early? Well, as just noted, Waymo has a careful and methodical approach to entering new markets, and Waymo vehicles will start arriving in Singapore in coming months to start autonomous vehicle testing, mapping, etc.

Singapore is a highly regulated place, but it’s also a super innovative country that likes to be at the forefront of technology and public policy. In a previous life when I was in the city & regional planning field, Singapore was a hotshot that got a lot of attention for its approach to planning, technology, and transportation. The government will, without a doubt, be very involved in Waymo’s testing and rollout, but it will also be keen to be ahead of the curve in this field.

“Waymo will need approval from Singapore’s Land Transport Authority (LTA) before it can begin accepting passengers. The city-state requires all autonomous vehicles to undergo a safety assessment conducted at the Centre of Excellence for Testing and Research (CETRAN) before they can be deployed on public roads,” The Verge shares. “The tests have been developed by LTA and CETRAN, with input from the Traffic Police. But Waymo isn’t totally unknown in Singapore. The company established a corporate entity there earlier this year and participates in Singapore’s Steering Committee on Autonomous Vehicles.”

Note that we’ve previously covered autonomous bus, autonomous shuttle, other autonomous shuttle, and autonomous streetsweeper progress in Singapore, among plenty of other cleantech matters.

data.title: Discounts on Kia EV9 Give It Ridiculous Price
data.description:
The Kia EV9 is one of the few three-row electric vehicles on the market. It’s quite large, and the interior and technology are very nice and high quality despite the vehicle being fairly affordable. However, apparently, it hasn’t been cheap enough — until some dealerships recently got aggressive with their discounting in order to move more off the lot.

According to Carscoops, a dealership in Texas is providing a $16,041 discount on the EV9 Light RWD, bringing it down from its starting MSRP of $54,900 to a ridiculously competitive $41,414. We’re talking the price of a Tesla Model 3, Tesla Model Y, or Kia Niro EV!

The EV9 Light RWD has only 230 miles of range, but that’s really plenty for the vast majority of buyers. And, yes, we’re talking about a large SUV that can seat up to 7 adults!

I’m personally not a fan of large vehicles, because I don’t like driving them, don’t feel a need for the extra space, and don’t like large vehicles taking up so much space and using so much energy, but this would be a hard deal to pass up or ignore!

There are big discounts on the EV9 elsewhere as well. “At Liberty Auto Plaza in Illinois, an EV Light Short Range has been handed a $15,000 discount, dropping the price from $57,480 to just $42,480,” Autoblog shares. “There’s also a $15k saving on the Light Long Range model, which nets you a more practical 304 miles between charges. This one’s price has been cut from $59,785 to $44,785.” Again, these are ridiculous prices for the large electric SUV. When you consider how much money the EV9 could save you in operational costs compared to a similarly spacious, 7-seat SUV powered by gasoline, the deals are even that much more enticing.

If you’ve been thinking about a Kia EV9 for a while, perhaps now is the time to jump! That is also, apparently, what many buyers have concluded this year so far. Sales of the electric model have been up 12% in the first 8 months of 2026 compared January–August of 2025.

data.title: Driven to Serve: How Taylor Searcy Turned Navy Service into Clean Energy Strategy at GM
data.description:
Most people don’t think about energy until the lights go out. Or transportation until the road is closed. Or the complex systems that keep people moving until they stop working.

Taylor Searcy has spent much of his career thinking about those systems.

Driven to Serve highlights the veterans and military-connected employees who build successful careers at GM with purpose and impact.

As a young Surface Warfare Officer aboard USS Lassen, he stood watch as Officer of the Deck, entrusted with the safe navigation of a $1 billion destroyer and more than 300 sailors. Every hour required situational awareness. Every decision carried consequences. Nothing worked unless the systems — and the people behind them — worked together.

Today, that same sense of responsibility extends beyond the bridge of USS Lassen.

As Clean Energy Strategy Lead at General Motors, Taylor works on the energy GM needs for its assembly plants, high-tech design centers, and offices. That includes helping the company support cleaner energy systems while balancing cost and reliability.

His view of that work grew from experience.

One of his first port visits aboard USS Lassen was to Dili, the capital of Timor-Leste, a Southeast Asian nation north of Australia. There, nightly blackouts showed him how deeply energy affects daily life.

Later, while researching sustainable maritime transportation in Fiji, he saw how remote island communities depended on infrequent visits from unreliable ships for access to goods and services. For many residents, it was their only link to the mainland.

Find out how Taylor connects Navy service, clean energy, and GM’s work today.

What did standing watch teach you about responsibility?

Standing watch taught me that responsibility is not about making every decision alone.

It is knowing what is in your authority, how the team operates, and when something needs to be escalated. As Officer of the Deck, I had to understand the full picture while also knowing when to rely on the chain of command.

That lesson has stayed with me. In any large organization, success depends on bringing the right people into the right decisions.

What Navy experience still helps you in your work today?

One thing I still rely on is building a plan around different courses of action, with contingencies in place from the start. That makes it easier to shift quickly when conditions change.

In the Navy, things moved quickly. Having a plan gave you a roadmap, but it did not mean everything would go exactly the way you expected. You had to think through different scenarios and be ready to adjust.

That still applies today. The work can be complex, so it helps to stay focused on the goal while staying flexible about how to get there.

Was there a moment when you realized how much people depend on reliable energy?

One of the experiences that stayed with me was my first port visit aboard USS Lassen to Dili, the capital of Timor-Leste.

The country had been through a long war for independence, and the electrical grid was still limited. At night, the power would go out regularly. I remember seeing that and realizing how much I had taken reliable, abundant energy for granted.

It wasn’t just about lights. It was about whether daily life could continue the way people needed it to.

I still think about that port visit. It made energy feel like something people depend on, not just something that runs in the background.

What made sustainability and clean energy feel like the right next step after the Navy?

I had been interested in sustainability for a long time, but the Navy made it feel more real.

I had seen places where resources were limited and damaged environments from overexploited resources. I had also seen how much effort it takes to keep ships fueled and operating at sea. That made me think more seriously about the nexus of sustainability and the energy systems people rely on every day.

After active duty, I wanted to do meaningful work that connected those experiences to something positive for people and the planet. That led me to a dual master’s degree program in Japan and Germany, and eventually to a small team in the South Pacific focused on sustainable maritime transportation.

Clean energy made sense to me because it touched the things I kept coming back to: the importance of resilience and interconnectedness of humanity and nature.

How does your work at GM connect energy and transportation?

GM uses a tremendous amount of energy to manufacture vehicles, so reliable and affordable power is essential to our operations.

My work helps GM support cleaner energy systems while managing cost and reliability. I’m really proud that GM secured enough renewable energy to match 100% of our U.S. electricity use in 2025, the first U.S. automaker to reach that milestone.

I also think of electric vehicles as more than a mode of transportation. They are becoming part of the broader energy system. For example, bidirectional charging technology can turn your compatible GM EV into a home backup generator.*

That makes GM’s role in the energy transition especially meaningful to me. Our purpose is to pioneer the innovations that move and connect people to what matters. I have seen what happens when communities lack dependable transportation or energy, so that purpose feels very real to me.

What would you tell other veterans who are looking for their next mission?

Clean energy and sustainability are broad fields. There is room for people with many different backgrounds.

I would tell veterans not to underestimate what they already know how to do. If you have served, you understand responsibility. You understand how to work through uncertainty. You understand what it means to be part of something larger than yourself.

Use your network. Reach out to other veterans. Ask questions. There is no single path into this work.

For me, the connection between the Navy and GM comes back to integrity. At the Naval Academy, I was grounded in the Navy’s core values of honor, courage, and commitment. GM’s behavior of “Win with Integrity” resonates with me because it carries that same idea forward.

The work changes. The mission can too. But the way you carry yourself matters most.

Discover more about how veterans and military-connected employees at GM turn service into impact.

  • Driven to Serve: How Army Reserve Service Guides Jhansi Nalla’s Leadership at GM
  • Driven to Serve: Rain Thompson on navigating life after the Navy
  • Driven to Serve: Brett Munster’s Marine confidence keeps GM moving
  • Driven to Serve: How Alex Reba supports two missions at once
  • Driven to Serve: How John Gillmer champions veterans and data at GM
  • Driven to Serve: Brandon Gifford still owns the mission at GM
  • Shifting Gears: Veterans transition from military service to vehicle service

*Requires a V2H-capable GM EV, GM Energy PowerShift charger and V2H Enablement Kit, a properly equipped home, and proper grid interconnection; performance and duration depend on battery state, weather, and load; not recommended for powering medical devices.

Article by GM.

data.title: BYD Planning 4 Factories in Europe
data.description:
BYD’s big focus at the moment seems to be finding ways to expand globally and grow its sales outside of China as fast as possible. The Chinese market is not the hottest, which is surely part of it, but it’s also clearly a prime time in the transition to electric vehicles and BYD is probably trying to ensure that it captures market share in countries around the world before it’s “too late” — or just much harder to break into a settled market.

Right now, there’s not much competition in most markets across Asia, South America, North America, and Africa. BYD is jumping into a bunch of countries on these continents and gobbling up new customers quickly. There’s already significant competition in Europe, but even in Europe, there are almost no markets where EVs have more than 50% of the market. It’s also a huge market for new-vehicle sales. So, one key target for BYD is the European market.

To help achieve its goals, now that the EU has high tariffs on EVs produced in China, BYD has to set up production facilities in Europe. The news this week is that BYD is planning on having three vehicle assembly plants in Europe and one battery factory there. That’s the plan for now, at least.

“BYD is ​currently starting production at its first ⁠European plant in Hungary and expects ​to decide by the end of the ​year on a second manufacturing site, Alfredo Altavilla told a presentation in Turin on Wednesday,” Reuters writes. “The ​company is looking to acquire and ​refurbish an existing facility rather than build a new ‌plant ⁠from scratch, with Spain and France among its preferred locations, he said.”

That’s currently the long-term plan. Though, naturally, if things go well, that long-term plan could grow; and if things go badly, perhaps BYD will downsize its plans. What do you think — is this plan too big, too small, or just right?

data.title: No Wonder The Tesla Cybercab Launch Was So Underwhelming
data.description:
It was a mystery wrapped in an enigma when Tesla CEO Elon Musk failed to show up for the much-anticipated launch of the company’s new Cybercab in Austin, Texas. Investors also greeted the September 3 event with a less than enthusiastic response, leading Tesla stock to sink throughout the following days. A rebound has occurred since then, but Tesla still has left some questions unanswered — 21 of them, to be exact.

Questions Swirl Around Cybercab Launch, Again

If the September 3 launch was meant to demonstrate Cybercab’s ability to steer itself through the streets of Austin without the benefit of a human operator, maybe it did, and maybe it didn’t. Tesla is pitching the Cybercab as a pure robotaxi, meaning it is designed without a steering wheel or any other sort of human-manipulated controls, though Motortrend is among the auto industry news organizations reporting that the Cybercab can indeed be operated manually, by virtue of a “secret” virtual joystick.

Musk has also been known to show off the forthcoming Optimus “autonomous” humanoid robot with a remote control assist from human operators, so there’s that.

Fully and completely autonomous or not, the September 3 Cybercab launch raised questions about first responder safety, among other concerns. More recently, the Cybercab has attracted a rash of pranksters jumping in front of the robotaxi to “prove” its autonomous driving system works.

Just one day after the Austin launch, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration also jumped in to remind everyone that the Cybercab is not necessarily ready for primetime. “The US Department of Transportation’s National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) today announced that it has opened an Audit Query (AQ) to investigate Tesla’s certification that its new Cybercab meets all applicable Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards (FMVSS),” NHTSA announced.

“NHTSA’s Audit Query will evaluate the technical data and processes Tesla relied upon to self-certify compliance for a vehicle lacking traditional human controls,” NHTSA added for emphasis.

To further cloud the rollout, earlier this week a Cybercab reportedly avoided a routine, 10-minute ride drive and instead chose a 70-minute detour, underscoring the technology’s unreadiness for highway travel.

“Was supposed to be a quick 10 minute hop from 99 Ranch to the Domain. The car had other plans and took me on a massive south detour through East Austin. Guess the Cybercab wanted the scenic route today. Total ride time was 70 minutes,” wrote Reddit poster TyGuy539 on r/Austin.

The Gloves Come Flying Off

Of course, Elon Musk himself oversaw the gutting of staff at NHTSA and other federal offices during his role as the chief of Trump’s budget-hacking “DOGE” office, so it’s unclear how much investigating NHTSA can actually do. Still, the office has some teeth left, and evidently Tesla still has some ‘splaining to do.

As part of the Audit Query, NHTSA issued a  “Special Order” that requires Tesla to submit the technical background supporting its Cybercab self-certification, under oath, by September 30.

“Based on information available to NHTSA, the Cybercab is a purpose-built vehicle that Tesla certified as compliant with all applicable Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards (FMVSS),” NHTSA reminds everyone, especially Tesla Head of Litigation Brian Jazeri and Tesla Associate General Counsel Eric Williams, to whom the Special Order is addressed.

“Self-certification is a foundational responsibility for vehicle manufacturers under the National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act of 1966 (Safety Act), as amended and recodified, 49 U.S.C. Chapter 30,” NHTSA further reminds.

The Special Order lists 21 specific requests for information. In terms of the September 3 demonstration in Austin, #5 is particularly interesting: “Confirm whether the subject vehicles are capable of being driven by a human driver using temporarily attached human driver controls.”

Request #6 is also of interest:

“State whether temporarily installed human driver controls or other equipment for use by a human driver were a part of Tesla’s basis for certifying compliance with any FMVSS. If so, describe the human driver controls and list the FMVSS for which the human driver controls were used as a part of Tesla’s basis for certifying compliance.”

Request #13 further indicates that NHTSA may have caught Tesla in a mistruth regarding the nature of the September 3 rollout.

“State whether the subject vehicles have a turn signal operative unit that is self- canceling by steering wheel rotation. Also state whether the subject vehicles have a manually operated control of a turn signal operating unit,” NHTSA demands, then continues:

“If the answer to any of the previous statements is no, provide in detail how Tesla determined that the subject vehicles complied with FMVSS No. 108 (49 CFR § 571.108) S9.1.1. If your answer differs depending on whether any human driver control or other equipment for use by a human driver is temporarily installed in the vehicle, describe in detail how it differs.”

Tesla Lives To See Another Day

Regardless of the Cybercab kerfluffle, Tesla has maintained its position as the #1 seller of EVs in the US. Other stakeholders were giving the automaker a run for the money until last year, when the premature death of the federal EV tax credit sparked an electrification pullback among Ford and General Motors, among others.

As reported by Kelly Blue Book earlier today, Tesla led other automakers in EV sales for August, with Toyota, Rivian, Hyundai, and Cadillac following up. However, Tesla sales in August were 3.8% lower than in July, while Toyota went up 34.9% in the same period.

More to the point, the overall EV sales picture in the US looks dim indeed, largely if not exclusively due to last year’s sharp U-turn in federal energy policy.

“New EV sales were up 2.5% from July, but down 46.9% from 2025,” KBB notes, referring to the numbers for August. EVs accounted for just 5.7% of new vehicle sales in the US in August, even as the global marketplace jumped to more than 25%.

All else being equal, Trump’s ill-fated war in Iran could help turn the sales slump around. Trump can also take part of the responsibility for enabling Russia to drag out its unprovoked invasion of Ukraine, which is also impacting global oil markets. The conflict was launched by Russian President Vladimir Putin in February of 2022, prompting Ukraine to attack Russia’s oil infrastructure in defense. The attacks have intensified since then, cutting deeply into Russia’s ability to export diesel and gasoline.

With all this in mind, Tesla has an opportunity to see its sales numbers increase over the coming months. Beyond that, it’s anybody’s guess. The new Ford Fathom electric pickup truck is still on track for volume production next year, and Rivian somehow managed to secure a $4.5 billion Energy Department loan to build a new factory in Georgia, among other signs of rising competition in the US market.

Photo: The Tesla Cybercab rollout in Austin, Texas has been colored by many questions, including a list of 21 specific demands for information from the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (courtesy of Tesla via CleanTechnica archive).

data.title: Farm Electrification Should Start With The Work, Not The Tractor
data.description:
Ask whether agriculture can electrify and the conversation usually arrives at the same machine within minutes: the tractor. More specifically, the large diesel tractor working hard through planting, harvest or another narrow seasonal window. It is a legitimate engineering challenge, but it is a poor organizing principle for farm electrification.

Farms do many kinds of work. Milk has to be cooled. Water has to be pumped. Livestock buildings need ventilation and heat. Greenhouses have thermal loads. Grain and other crops may need drying. Chemicals have to be applied across fields. Refrigeration and processing equipment run at fixed locations. Some machinery returns to the same yard every few hours; other equipment may have to work nearly continuously while weather and crop conditions cooperate.

Those services have different energy quantities, power requirements, timing constraints and infrastructure needs. The fact that a large battery tractor cannot yet replace every 200-horsepower diesel machine says almost nothing about whether a kerosene heater, irrigation pump or milk chiller should still be burning fossil fuels.

That is the strategic mistake I wanted to correct in an updated assessment of farm electrification. My earlier CleanTechnica analysis grew out of Ireland’s fuel protests and the vulnerability created by agricultural dependence on diesel. The wider conclusion is more useful: good farm-electrification strategy should begin with the work the farm needs performed, not with a shopping list of electric equipment.

The full TFIE Strategy Briefing develops that work-first framework across dairy, irrigation, greenhouses, broadacre farming and smallholder productive access. It looks at what should electrify now, where the machine itself should change, when electrical infrastructure has to come first, and when retaining existing diesel equipment is still the rational choice.

Consider solar on a dairy farm. Teagasc’s 2025 solar guide models a 100-cow farm consuming about 25,000 kWh annually and a 25 kWp solar array producing 23,484 kWh. On annual accounting, that looks close to energy independence: generation equals about 94% of consumption. Yet without a battery, the model uses only 30% of the PV generation on site. Add a 12.5 kWh battery and self-consumption rises to 45%, but under the modeled tariffs the unsubsidized simple payback actually worsens from eight years to ten.

That little example contains most of the discipline the sector needs. Annual energy balance is not the same as useful energy delivery. Higher self-consumption is not automatically a better investment. A battery should solve a defined problem—peak demand, backup, charging support, network constraints or a meaningful tariff spread—not simply make the self-consumption percentage look prettier.

Stationary thermal loads can offer much cleaner cases. A Teagasc pig-farm example from 2016 involved an 800-sow operation burning around 900 litres of kerosene every week for farrowing and weaner heating. The reported heat-pump installation cost €58,000 including installation and reduced annual energy costs from about €46,800 to €12,800, for a simple payback of roughly 20 months before financing. Those are decade-old prices and should not be used as a 2026 investment case, but the example still illustrates the underlying point: some apparently agricultural fossil-fuel problems are simply conventional stationary heating loads for which mature electric alternatives have existed for years.

Irrigation provides another example of why the service matters more than the machine. India has already deployed solar pumping at substantial scale. The official PM-KUSUM dashboard reported 711,133 standalone solar pumps installed under Component B and 841,081 pumps solarized through feeder-level Component C as of July 31, 2026.

But the service is not “operate a solar pump.” It is deliver the required volume of water at the required pressure and time without exhausting the resource. Pumping schedules and water storage can sometimes substitute for battery storage, while variable-speed drives can alter both energy consumption and operating flexibility. And because solar reduces the marginal energy cost of pumping, poorly governed systems can increase groundwater withdrawals rather than merely replace diesel. FAO has examined that groundwater risk, which means pumping technology, energy pricing and water governance have to be considered together.

Mobile machinery requires the same discipline. Fendt’s e107 Vario provides a useful commercial reality check precisely because its specifications are bounded rather than magical. The tractor has a 100 kWh battery, 55 kW of continuous power and 66 kW peak output. Fendt says it can work for roughly four to seven hours in partial-load applications such as mechanical weed control or planting, while energy-intensive transport reduces runtime.

That is not evidence that electric tractors do not work. It is evidence that duty cycle is the question. An electric tractor capable of a full day of lighter specialist work can be commercially useful without being able to replace every high-energy diesel operation. Conversely, rated horsepower tells us surprisingly little about whether a machine is electrifiable. Energy used for the actual task, charging opportunities, return-to-base patterns, completion windows and the cost of downtime matter much more.

Electrification can also change the machine itself. Spraying does not intrinsically require several tonnes of tractor to cross every hectare merely because that is how the job evolved around diesel engines, hydraulics and human drivers. Agricultural drones, smaller autonomous equipment and distributed machines can sometimes substitute a different architecture for the historical one. The right comparison is still the complete service, including batteries, support vehicles, operators, refilling, water, application quality and repeat passes—not a propulsion-only comparison.

Heavy seasonal work remains genuinely difficult. A paid-off diesel tractor doing relatively few hours annually but occasionally facing extreme workloads may be economically sensible to retain. Replacing it early can become particularly unattractive if the electric alternative also requires expensive batteries and a major rural connection upgrade. That is not a failure of an electrification strategy. It is what a strategy looks like when replacement timing and capital utilization are included.

There is a corresponding infrastructure trap. Rural grid connections, transformers and charging capacity can take longer to plan and build than machinery takes to procure. Farms that wait until the ideal electric machine exists before thinking about electricity supply can discover that the machine is available years before the connection it needs.

That means some infrastructure should move ahead of equipment. A dairy upgrading electrical capacity for heat pumps, refrigeration and hot water can create headroom for later machinery charging. Contractor depots are especially interesting because they concentrate expensive equipment and annual operating hours. Higher utilization can make costly electric machinery easier to amortize, while one substantial grid connection, charging system or battery buffer can support equipment serving many farms.

Contractors do not magically solve the problem. Several customers may all need the same machine during the same three-day weather window, and high utilization increases the cost of downtime. But ownership structure belongs in the analysis. The best owner of an expensive electric agricultural machine may be a service business rather than the farm whose land it works.

Different agricultural systems therefore produce different sequences. Dairy and intensive livestock operations may find cooling, hot water, ventilation, heat recovery and pumps at the front of the queue. Irrigated agriculture may start with pumping efficiency, scheduling, water storage and power supply. Greenhouses are more thermal. Broadacre systems can have relatively little stationary fuel use but enormous seasonal mobile peaks. Smallholders without much productive energy access may gain more by adding refrigeration, irrigation or processing than by replacing an existing fossil-fuel machine.

Policy should follow those binding constraints rather than simply count subsidized machines. If connection capacity prevents viable projects, reinforce the distribution system. If equipment economics depend on utilization, make contractors and shared-service businesses eligible. If solar irrigation creates groundwater risks, coordinate energy support with water governance. If storage does not provide an economically valuable service, do not pretend that increasing PV self-consumption is sufficient justification.

The useful measure of agricultural electrification is not the date when the final diesel tractor disappears. It is whether successive equipment replacements, infrastructure investments and operating changes reduce fossil-fuel exposure while preserving—or improving—the cost and reliability of producing food.

The tractor will electrify when the combination of batteries, duty cycles, infrastructure and economics makes sense. Plenty of the rest of the farm should not have to wait for it.

Read the complete work-based strategy, operating-context analysis and evidence in TFIE Strategy Briefing.

data.title: Stellantis BOW Takes Autonomous Delivery to The Next Level
data.description:
HANOVER, Germany — Among the many electric vehicles at IAA Transportation 2026, the Stellantis BOW is hard to miss.

It is small, green and looks nothing like a conventional delivery van. There is no cab and no driver’s seat. The cargo body sits over four wheels, with cameras and sensors built into the vehicle, including a prominent sensor unit on the roof.

BOW stands for Box-on-Wheels. Stellantis Pro One developed the autonomous electric vehicle with UQI Robotics as a concept for moving goods without a driver. The idea is aimed at the last mile, but Stellantis is also looking at places where the vehicle can operate in a more controlled environment. Factories, hospitals and airports are among the possible applications.

A vehicle running around an airport or a factory has a much easier job than one sent into the middle of a European city. Its operating area can be defined, routes can be mapped and the number of things it has to deal with can be limited.

Stellantis is using BOW to look at what happens when an electric commercial vehicle is designed around autonomous operation from the beginning rather than starting with a conventional van and adding automated driving equipment.

There is no need to accommodate a driver, so the space inside can be used for cargo. The vehicle is essentially a mobile box with the hardware needed to move it around.

At this stage, Stellantis is not giving BOW a full set of production specifications. There is no announced battery size, range, payload capacity, maximum speed or charging time. It is a development project, not a production vehicle.

That also means some of the numbers circulating around concept vehicles should be treated carefully. There is no reason to assume that BOW uses the battery, motor or other components of one of Stellantis’ existing electric vans.

UQI Robotics is responsible for much of the autonomous and robotics technology being explored in the project. Stellantis brings the commercial-vehicle side, including its experience with fleet customers and logistics.

The partnership is looking at how the vehicle could fit into an actual delivery operation rather than simply demonstrating that an autonomous vehicle can drive from one point to another.

A delivery vehicle normally requires someone to drive it from the depot to the customer and back again. If the driving part can eventually be automated, the logistics operation can be organized around the movement of the goods rather than the working hours of the driver. But that is still a considerable step away.

Autonomous driving in a controlled industrial site is one thing. Sending a driverless vehicle through a city with pedestrians, bicycles, parked cars, roadworks and unpredictable traffic is another.

Stellantis is therefore treating BOW as a way of testing the concept and its possible applications. There is no production timetable yet. What makes it stand out at IAA is the design. Most of the electric commercial vehicles on display are recognizably vans or trucks that have been converted to battery power. BOW starts with a different assumption, because there is no reason for it to look like a van if nobody is going to sit in the van.

That is about as far as Stellantis is taking the idea for now. The company has the vehicle at IAA, it is demonstrating the autonomous technology and it is working with UQI Robotics to see where the concept can make sense commercially. But standing in front of BOW at IAA, it is clear what Stellantis is experimenting with: not simply an electric delivery van, but a delivery vehicle in which the driver has disappeared from the design.

data.title: Lynk & Co 08 EM-P Reaches 200,000 Global Deliveries
data.description:
Since its official launch in September 2023, the Lynk & Co 08 EM-P has built a strong reputation through its performance, capabilities and customer acclaim. Expanding from the Chinese market to the global stage, the model has now achieved 200,000 cumulative deliveries worldwide, with a presence across more than 30 countries and regions in Europe, Asia-Pacific, Latin America and North Africa. In the first half of 2026, the model ranked among the top three best-selling vehicles in its segment in overseas markets including Mexico and Morocco.

Over the past three years, the Lynk & Co 08 EM-P has continuously demonstrated its capabilities through a series of demanding challenges. In terms of range, the model set two Guinness World Records: completing the longest distance driven by a plug-in hybrid SUV without refuelling or recharging, covering 1,813 km between Xining and Hami in China; and achieving the longest pure electric range for a plug-in hybrid SUV, travelling 293 km in Toluca, Mexico.

The Lynk & Co 08 EM-P has also successfully completed long-distance expeditions through some of the world’s most challenging environments. It travelled more than 7,000 km in 14 days from Yining in Xinjiang, China to the Arctic Circle, enduring temperatures as low as -30°C. The vehicle also served as the official expedition vehicle for the QUEST DAKAR 2026 Rally, crossing borders between three African countries and covering 3,200 km of desert terrain in temperatures reaching 41°C, further validating its adaptability and reliability in extreme conditions.

The model has earned a series of prestigious international awards. In design, it received the 2024 Red Dot Product Design Award. In safety, it achieved a five-star Euro NCAP rating in September 2025 and recorded the highest overall score among plug-in hybrid vehicles tested that year. In the market, it has also been recognised with honours such as “Best Luxury Plug-in Hybrid SUV of the Year” in Mexico and Morocco’s AIVAM Car of the Year 2026 award. From range and safety performance to professional certifications and customer recognition, the Lynk & Co 08 EM-P has demonstrated its competitiveness on a global scale.

The true measure of quality is reflected in long-term customer trust. Lynk & Co 08 EM-P owners worldwide have collectively driven more than 4.4 billion kilometres, while the highest-mileage individual vehicle has exceeded 540,000 kilometres. The model’s active safety systems have helped prevent more than 400,000 potential accidents.

This trust continues to grow through direct customer experiences. Recently, a group of Lynk & Co 08 EM-P owners from Kazakhstan travelled to China to visit Geely’s Global Safety Centre and the Yuyao manufacturing plant, where they experienced first-hand the vehicle’s intelligent production processes, rigorous testing procedures and globally consistent quality standards.

With its combination of advanced electrified performance, intelligent cockpit technologies, comprehensive safety features and premium quality, the Lynk & Co 08 EM-P has established itself as a highly regarded intelligent hybrid SUV for modern families around the world.

About Lynk & Co International

Lynk & Co is more than a car company; it’s an innovative mobility provider. Offering a diverse range of electrified cars – from the long-range plug-in hybrid 08, to the fully electric 02, to the popular plug-in hybrid 01 – the brand combines vibrant, cutting-edge design with pioneering connectivity solutions to deliver a forward-thinking driving experience. Established in 2016 and headquartered in Gothenburg, Sweden, Lynk & Co now operates in 25 markets across Europe and is on an ambitious expansion journey, redefining what modern mobility can be.

As Lynk & Co continues its bold journey of expanding into retail sales channels through partnerships with local retailers, more than 140 partner-operated sales points are now open across Europe. This growing network brings Lynk & Co closer to more customers while staying true to its mission: to change the future of mobility – for people, for progress, and for impact

data.title: New Life For EV Charging Stations Trump Tried To Kill
data.description:
“A crushingly stupid waste of taxpayer dollars” is only one way to sum up the current state of the US government, but it’s a good one. When President Donald Trump took office last year, he hacked away at numerous federal plans and programs, some of which have already been restored by court order after a series of expensive legal battles. One such example is the “NEVI” public EV charging program, which Trump tried — and failed — to kill.

The NEVI Public EV Charging Plan In A Nutshell

NEVI is short for the National Electric Vehicle Infrastructure program, a $5 billion EV charging plan funded through a carve-out from the 2021 Bipartisan Infrastructure Law. NEVI provides state transportation planners with federal dollars to build public fast-charging stations in priority locations. The goal is to encourage EV uptake by ensuring that long-distance drivers can rely on a coordinated, national network of fast-charging stations, located on interstate highways and other major arteries.

Some states intentionally dragged their feet on NEVI planning. Others lagged due to a shortfall in staffing and other resources. Identifying suitable locations was also a challenge for some states. However, three years after the BIL passed, all 50 states had submitted their NEVI plans. In addition, eight states were already installing NEVI-funded EV charging stations.

By July of 2024, 61 charging ports were in operation and another 2,500 ports were in the pipeline. Nevertheless, upon taking office in January of 2025, Trump ordered the US Department of Transportation to suspend the NEVI program.

That was a surprise to Pennsylvania, for example. “On February 26, just 20 days after Trump suspended NEVI, the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation celebrated the official opening of three additional NEVI-funded stations,” CleanTechnica reported, noting that PennDOT officials made an extra effort to inform everyone that NEVI paid for the new charging stations. With the three new additions, Pennsylvania had a total of eight NEVI-funded stations up and running by February last year.

I Want My NEVI!

Some states took the NEVI suspension lying down. Others sprang into action. On August 1 of 2025, a group of states filed a lawsuit against Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy and the administrator of the Federal Highway Administration, Gloria M. Shepherd, demanding re-activation of the NEVI funds.

“President Trump has unleashed an attack on an increasingly popular consumer choice—the electric vehicle,” the lawsuit reads, citing Trump’s executive order titled, “Unleashing American Energy.”

The EO established elimination of the “electric vehicle (EV) mandate” as US policy. However, the plaintiffs note that the US government “never adopted any such ‘EV mandate.’”

More to the point, the lawsuit describes how Trump broke the law — namely, the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law — when he directed the Federal Highway Administration to suspend the NEVI program.

“Pursuant to 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(B) and 28 U.S.C. § 2201, Plaintiff States are entitled to a declaration that the Defendants’ actions to categorically ‘suspend’ or revoke all State Electric Vehicle Infrastructure Deployment Plan approvals and to categorically withhold or withdraw NEVI Formula Program funds violate the Take Care Clause,” the lawsuit concludes, requiring to the President’s Constitutional duty to “take care that the laws be faithfully executed.”

Apparently the whole thing was a misunderstanding. Duffy didn’t really mean to prevent states from using their Congressionally mandated dollars to build EV charging stations. Just a few days after the lawsuit was filed, on August 11 the Department of Transportation posted a press release headlined, “President Trump’s Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy Unveils Revised NEVI Guidance to Allow States to Actually Build EV Chargers.”

Errr…whut?

“U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy today unveiled revised guidance for the National Electric Vehicle Infrastructure (NEVI) Formula Program. The updates streamline applications, provide states with more flexibility, and slash red tape left by the Biden-Buttigieg Administration,” DOT explained.

“This will ensure charging stations are actually built,” DOT emphasized.

Okay, Sean. You do you. EV charging stations were already “actually” being built, but perhaps he didn’t get the memo.

NEVI In Motion

Despite Duffy’s suggestion that Trump would “actually” accelerate the NEVI-funded network, the August 11 announcement was largely just another public relations exercise. As noted by the legal news organization Leg1, staffing cuts at the Transportation Department slowed down the administration of the program. Cuts at the Energy Department also impeded progress, which was involved in the NEVI program through the Joint Office of Energy and Transportation — which also suffered cuts.

Additionally, under the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026, Duffy took almost $1 billion in un-disbursed NEVI funds and other NEVI-related programs, and transferred them to other highway programs. The action included NEVI funds that were earmarked for maintenance and repair costs.

Nevertheless, NEVI soldiers on. On September 14, the North Carolina Department of Transportation issued a brief announcement describing a new round of NEVI awards, adding seven new locations to the five stations funded in 2024, before Trump took office.

North Carolina received a $109 million share of the NEVI pot. This week’s activity covered $14.4 million of the total.

“By expanding our electric vehicle charging network, we’re making it easier for everyone to travel confidently across the state, while supporting a cleaner, more modern transportation economy,” enthused NCDOT’s State Initiatives Manager Heather Hildebrandt.

NCDOT expects its share of NEVI funding to cover a three-year build-out program. The next step in the state’s electric mobility plan will bring EV charging stations to rural areas and other communities that don’t necessarily sit on major transportation arteries.

Another Day, Another 6oo EV Charging Stations, Another #TrumpFail

Trump’s war against the “EV mandate” certainly did throttle down momentum in the US vehicle electrification movement. However, in typical Trump fashion, he then launched a war of choice against Iran, which continues to spin out in the form of upward-spiraling fuel prices, motivating more drivers to research EV alternatives.

Whether or not all that EV-curious activity levels up to an EV sales recovery remains to be seen. However, in some jurisdictions drivers won’t have much of a choice. New York City, for example, is adding 600 more curbside charging stations to its current roster of 88, in support of a phased-in municipal mandate requiring all drivers licensed by the Taxi and Limousine Commission to use zero emission or wheelchair-accessible vehicles.

Image: Trump tried, and failed, to stop states from building new public EV charging stations along major transportation arteries with funds from the federal NEVI program (GIS map of EV charging stations courtesy of NCDOT).

data.title: Building Waymo’s Risk & Insurance Foundation in Europe with Allianz Partners
data.description:
Over years of operating a commercial rider-only service across the U.S. — serving more than half a million paid trips weekly — we have learned that bringing autonomous driving technology to new regions requires building a robust ecosystem of trusted, local partners. As we look toward our commercial expansion in Europe — beginning with our initial deployment plans in London and Munich — we are teaming up with Allianz Partners to establish the insurance, claims, and safety research foundation needed to scale across the continent.

To deliver a seamless and reliable service, building a strong operational backbone is just as critical as developing advanced autonomous driving technology. That includes establishing a comprehensive risk, insurance, and digital claims infrastructure. Backed by real-world safety data showing 16x reduction in serious injury crashes compared to human drivers in cities where we operate, this partnership reflects Waymo’s deliberate approach to responsible, scaled deployment. Through this collaboration, Allianz Partners will support Waymo fleets across Europe with:

  • Insurance & risk solutions: Tailored coverage and risk management for Waymo’s autonomous fleet, including fleet insurance, liability protection, and new insurance models designed for autonomous mobility.
  • Claims ecosystem: Digital claims handling and management.
  • Research & safety collaboration: Joint research initiatives with the Allianz Center for Technology, exploring high-priority tropics across crash analysis, safety modeling, and risk evaluation.

Additionally, the companies will explore potential new areas of collaboration over time, including innovative operational solutions to streamline vehicle recovery tailored for autonomous fleets.

“Autonomous mobility is one of the most significant shifts our industry will navigate in the years ahead. Waymo’s technology leadership, combined with Allianz’s global expertise in insurance, assistance, and vehicle safety, allows us to build a comprehensive ecosystem that gives operators and passengers confidence at every stage of the journey.” — says Tomas Kunzmann, CEO, Allianz Partners.

“As we advance our commercial rollout in Europe, building the right operational foundation is just as critical as the technology behind the Waymo Driver. Teaming up with Allianz Partners allows us to pair our proven U.S. safety record and commercial experience with world-class European risk and claims expertise, ensuring we scale reliably and responsibly from day one.” — says Tilia Gode, Head of Risk & Insurance at Waymo.

Introducing autonomous ride-hailing internationally is a deliberate process. Working alongside Allianz Partners ensures we have the local expertise and operational strength needed to introduce the Waymo Driver safely, reliably, and responsibly as we grow in Europe.
